items.title: Red Tape Theory™: Just Because We Can Does Not Mean We Should — A Study of Generative AI, Creative Utility, and Brand Appropriateness
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has rapidly reduced the distance between imagining a creative artifact and producing it. Images, videos, written works, advertisements, illustrations, and other forms of media that once required substantial time, labor, technical expertise, or financial resources can now be generated with comparatively little production effort. This paper examines the distinction between whether something can be produced and whether producing it is appropriate, useful, accurate, relevant, or communicatively successful. Using the framework of Red Tape Theory™, the paper investigates the proposition: Just because we can does not mean we should. The proposition is not presented as an argument against artificial intelligence, generative media, or technological experimentation. Rather, it examines the possibility that increased technological capability can create a tendency to treat capability itself as justification for use. The paper develops a series of distinctions: CAPABILITY ≠ APPROPRIATENESSNOVELTY ≠ VALUETECHNICAL QUALITY ≠ COMMUNICATIVE SUCCESSBEAUTY ≠ ACCURACYATTENTION ≠ UNDERSTANDINGPRODUCTION EFFICIENCY ≠ CREATIVE JUSTIFICATIONCAN ≠ SHOULD Three observational contexts are examined. First, the author’s use of generative AI across different creative tasks demonstrates the importance of task-dependent utility and tool selection. OpenAI systems have been used for conceptual development, thesis writing, philosophical exploration, poetry, and children’s literature, while other generative systems have been used for more straightforward visual-production tasks. This comparison is presented not as a universal ranking of AI systems, but as an example of a tool-agnostic, purpose-first approach to creative technology. Second, publicly documented NFL–Adobe implementations of generative AI are examined as an example of AI being incorporated into a large-scale brand and content ecosystem. The case illustrates how generative technology can be used for content scaling, personalization, workflow efficiency, governance, and brand-oriented production while simultaneously raising questions about the relationship between technical possibility and communicative relevance. Third, the paper examines brand appropriateness and the possibility that an artifact may be technically sophisticated while remaining poorly aligned with the identity, purpose, audience, or context for which it was created. The paper proposes that creative evaluation should distinguish at least five dimensions: Capability — Can the system produce the requested artifact?Accuracy — Does the artifact correctly represent its subject?Quality — Is the artifact technically and aesthetically successful?Relevance — Does it serve the communication objective?Appropriateness — Does it belong within the brand and audience context? These dimensions should not be collapsed into a single judgment of whether an artifact is simply “good.” Within Red Tape Theory™, the resulting decision process is: PURPOSE → AUDIENCE → IDEA → TOOL → OUTPUT → OBSERVATION → QUESTION → ADJUSTMENT rather than: CAPABILITY → FIND SOMETHING TO USE IT FOR The paper further examines the consequences of reduced production friction. When generative systems make experimentation inexpensive, the number of possible creative artifacts can expand faster than the human capacity to evaluate them. The resulting abundance may increase the importance of creative judgment, taste, selection, restraint, and purpose rather than eliminate the need for them. The central argument is therefore not that AI should or should not be used. It is that technological capability does not independently establish creative justification. A system may produce something extraordinary without that extraordinary artifact being appropriate to the task. A generated image may be beautiful while inaccurately representing a product.A video may be technically impressive while confusing its audience.A campaign may generate enormous quantities of content while weakening the identity it was intended to reinforce.A novel visual concept may attract attention without communicating its intended meaning. The relevant question is consequently not simply: “What can this technology do?” but: “What are we trying to accomplish, and does this technology help us accomplish it?” Red Tape Theory™ treats these conditions as an observation problem rather than an automatic verdict. Audience discomfort does not by itself prove creative failure, just as technical sophistication does not by itself prove creative success. The relationship between purpose, artifact, audience response, and interpretation must remain open to investigation. The paper concludes that as production becomes easier, creative judgment becomes more important rather than less important. The technology can create the possibility. The human must still determine whether the possibility serves the purpose. YOU CANNOT FORCE AN AXIOM.™

items.title: Red Tape Theory™: Observer ≠ Interpreter — Author, Tool, and the Problem of Artificial Participation
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence has complicated familiar distinctions between creator and instrument. When a human interacts with a generative system to produce an artifact, the resulting process may involve human intention, artificial interpretation, system-generated material, human observation, selection, revision, and final judgment. This paper examines that process through three central propositions of Red Tape Theory™: Observer ≠ Interpreter.Author ≠ Tool.Tool ≠ Nothing. The first distinction separates observation from interpretation. An observer may establish that an event occurred without thereby establishing its meaning, cause, or intention. The second distinguishes authorship from instrumentation: the presence of a tool does not, by itself, determine authorship. The third prevents the opposite error of treating a tool as inconsequential simply because it is not classified as an author. The paper develops several related distinctions: Observation ≠ InterpretationParticipation ≠ AuthorshipContribution ≠ AgencyGeneration ≠ IntentionArtifact ≠ ProcessRepresentation ≠ Reality Rather than attempting to determine whether artificial intelligence should universally be considered an author, this paper examines what can be observed about human and artificial participation in AI-assisted creative processes. The central proposition is: A tool can participate without becoming an author, and an author can use a tool without becoming indistinguishable from the tool. The paper argues that attribution should begin with observation of the production process rather than with a predetermined classification of the technology involved. The framework does not attempt to establish whether artificial systems possess consciousness, intention, personhood, or independent agency. Those are separate questions. Instead, it asks a narrower question: what happened between the human, the tool, and the resulting artifact? Red Tape Theory™ therefore returns to its central methodological principle: Observe the process. Record the contribution. Distinguish the roles. Then interpret. YOU CANNOT FORCE AN AXIOM™.
